endorsements.title: CHAI Responsible AI Guide (Assurance Standards Guide)
endorsements.quote: Tracking tools embedded within a provider’s or AI vendor’s environment, which may not always be known or discovered absent specific due diligence, pose risk, and these risks are enhanced when combined with the power of AI tools.

endorsements.title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework: Generative AI Profile (NIST AI 600-1)
endorsements.issuer: National Institute of Standards and Technology
endorsements.quote: Implement a use-cased based supplier risk assessment framework to evaluate and monitor third-party entities’ performance and adherence to content provenance standards and technologies to detect anomalies and unauthorized changes; services acquisition and value chain risk management; and legal compliance.

commentary.bottom_line: No study supplied here tests whether pre-engagement privacy, security, supply-chain, or generative AI risk assessments of third-party AI vendors reduce harm, and no study documents the hazard itself. The recommendation currently rests on two framework endorsements, the CHAI Assurance Standards Guide and NIST AI 600-1, both phrased as "should."

perspectives.view: The evidence base contains zero studies testing the practice and zero studies documenting the hazard. Under GRADE conventions, certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence, and the effect of vendor risk assessment on privacy breaches, security incidents, or harmful outputs remains unmeasured. Framework endorsements reflect expert consensus and do not substitute for outcome data.

Two frameworks endorse the practice at the "should" level. CHAI states that vendor tracking tools may go undiscovered without specific due diligence. NIST AI 600-1 calls for a use-case-based supplier risk assessment covering content provenance, value chain risk, and legal compliance. Neither source is binding, and neither cites outcome evidence in the excerpts supplied.

commentary.research_gap: Studies are needed that compare health systems or procurements with and without structured pre-engagement AI vendor risk assessment and that measure downstream privacy incidents, security events, intellectual property disputes, and harmful generative outputs. Descriptive work documenting how often unassessed vendor AI introduces these problems in health care would also establish the size of the hazard.
commentary.underserved_note: No test of the practice exists, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Health systems cannot determine from this evidence whether vendor assessments address risks that may fall differently on these groups, such as data sharing with third parties or generative outputs in languages other than English.
